title: Pain Isn't the Problem
html:
2025

Everything, everywhere, all at once.

My emotional nuts were getting kicked in repeatedly, and I was, metaphorically speaking, doubled over, rolling around on the floor, waiting for them to drop back into place.

One day, I described my state to my brother, and he asked me,

“Well… what are you going to do about it?”

Taking a breath, swarms of hypotheticals buzzed around my mind.

Chaos…

Then quiet.

The hypotheticals vanished, leaving behind nothing but a wisp of anxiety and a clarifying realization:

Some interpret pain as a problem. Others interpret pain as a signal.

Embedded in the question “What are you going to do about it?” is the assumption that pain is a problem to be solved, and that it’s a problem that can be solved.

But what if it isn’t?

When we interpret pain as a problem, we avoid it—pushing away the difficult feelings because we think it’s bad to feel bad. We judge our feelings, assigning positive or negative value to them.

Suppressing, avoiding, and neglecting our emotions comes as naturally to us as breathing, just as it is natural for us to yank our hand away from a hot stove. But, in doing so, we forgo the maturation that occurs on the other side of, and within, discomfort. To be unwilling to feel is to be unwilling to grow.

However, when we interpret pain as a signal, we learn. Pain is a teacher, and it will guide you if you let it. Sometimes, it leads us outwards, towards action. Maybe your finger hurts because there’s a splinter in it, or you have a headache because you’re dehydrated, or your foot hurts because you’ve had a broken bone in it for 18 months because your mom didn’t want to take you to the doctor after you got hurt and couldn’t walk on it (but that’s crazy and would totally never happen, right?… love you mom☺️). It’s in these cases where “What are you going to do about it?” is the right question to ask. But, oftentimes, pain isn’t so kind, and its directions are less clear. Oftentimes, it merely acts as a mirror, reflecting truths that are, at times, too difficult to bear. What, then, can we do about it when doing isn’t the answer?

In such cases, all we can ever do is accept.

We take it all in, telling ourselves, “I’m hurting, and that’s okay.”

Life is riddled with injuries so profound that there is no recovering—just accepting. Father Time barrels onward without regard for what stands before him—taking from us our friends, parents, brothers and sisters, and children. No amount of chopping wood or hot yoga can salve such wounds. We cannot tweeze away the splinters of heartbreak, betrayal, and death. We can only be with them, and let them be—allowing them dissolve into our bodies and become a part of us forever.

Discerning whether pain calls for action or acceptance can spare us hours, even decades, of unnecessary psychological suffering, and it can unlock new states of equanimity that we may not have known possible. It’s astounding the degree of psychological freedom we can experience when we realize that, oftentimes, there isn’t any problem to solve. Most importantly, we can make this realization even while immersed in intense pain.

2025 was a bit of a doozy for me.

Here’s hoping 2026 will be a little brighter.

Wishing you all love and laughter,

Charlie 💙
